Trend Micro works continuously, using automated mechanisms with a maximum five-minute delay in detection and alerts the system administrator via email when an anomaly is detected. Logs are checked on a daily basis to see if there are any anomalies. VGC Security Engineer has configured FirePOWER (by enabling intrusion rules and defining thresholds) to fire when unauthorized components/devices are detected. FirePOWER automatically notifies the FTGS Security team via email when unauthorized components/devices are introduced into the environment.<br/>The VGC Security Engineer has configured Tripwire to automatically notify the FTGS Security team when unauthorized components/devices are detected. To do this, the VGC Security Engineer baselines each customer environment so that any changes to the baseline trigger an alert.<br/>The VGC Security Engineer also configures Splunk alert by defining the appropriate Splunk event code/event ID for unauthorized components/device detection, saving the custom search as an alert and defining the trigger/alerting threshold.<br/>**IL4 Implementation:** Same as VGC implementation.</td>
        <td></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>Part b</td>
        <td>**Implemented**<br/>**Service Provider Corporate**<br/>**VGC:** If VGC Security Engineers or System Administrators are alerted that unauthorized components have been added to the system, VGC Security Engineers or System Administrators immediately alert the VGC Program Manager, who notifies the VGC CPM Customer Administrator via email. The VGC System Administrator and Security Engineer file an incident report, which is stored in VGC’s internal FedRAMP OneDrive repository. In addition, the VGC Network Administrator and Security Engineer disable network access for the unauthorized component or device by blocking ports and protocols or disabling appropriate services used by the unauthorized component during its network access attempt.<br/>**IL4 Implementation:** DoD-affiliated agency customers takes the following actions when unauthorized components are detected: disables network access by such components; isolates the components; notifies the ISSO and ISSM and others as the local organization deems appropriate.</td>
        <td></td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

The VGC System Administrator configures automation tools such as BigFix and RHEL Satellite to automate discovery and deployment of new patches for open source software for vendors whose libraries are included as part of BigFix and RHEL Satellite repositories. For vendors whose libraries are not included in BigFix and RHEL Satellite</td>
        <td>patching is done manually. <br/><br/> ● **Network and firewall compatibility** – The VGC Network Administrator works with the VGC Security Engineer to determine whether the risk is low enough to justify opening ports for open source software. At a minimum the following default security settings are changed: <br/> - Default user names and passwords <br/> - Strengthen authentication mechanisms <br/> - Disable non-critical services and programs bundled with the open source software <br/> - Apply access control and permissions based on role <br/><br/> ● **Test and scan** – The VGC System Administrator</td>

        <td>and VGC Security Engineer configure Nessus to perform authenticated vulnerability scans on the open source software to uncover any vulnerabilities such as missing patches</td>
        <td>enabled unsecure services</td>

The policies are reviewed and updated by the VGC Security Engineer, the VGC Security Analyst, and the VGC Program Manager at least every three years. After the policy review has been complete, the Security Analyst sends an email to the VGC ISSO and Program Manager documenting the Policies that have been reviewed, the date of the review and the changes that have been made. Once the VGC ISSO agrees with the changes made, the Security Analyst is responsible for updating the Policies and uploading them to the VGC’s internal FedRAMP OneDrive Repository. They are located in VGC’s internal FedRAMP OneDrive Repository, are emailed only to authorized personnel upon request, and are available for 3PAO review.<br/>**IL4 Implementation:** Same as VGC however for DoD-affiliated customer agency all stakeholders identified in the contingency plan.</td>

### CP-2 Contingency Plan (L) (M) (H)
The organization:
(a) Develops a contingency plan for the information system that:
* (3) Identifies essential missions and business functions and associated contingency requirements;
* (4) Provides recovery objectives, restoration priorities, and metrics;
* (5) Addresses contingency roles, responsibilities, assigned individuals with contact information;
* (6) Addresses maintaining essential missions and business functions despite an information system disruption, compromise, or failure;
* (7) Addresses eventual, full information system restoration without deterioration of the security safeguards originally planned and implemented; and

(8) Is reviewed and approved by [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles];

(g) Distributes copies of the contingency plan to [Assignment: organization-defined key contingency personnel (identified by name and/or by role) and organizational elements];

(h) Coordinates contingency planning activities with incident handling activities;

(i) Reviews the contingency plan for the information system [FedRAMP Assignment: at least annually];

(j) Updates the contingency plan to address changes to the organization, information system, or environment of operation and problems encountered during contingency plan implementation, execution, or testing;

(k) Communicates contingency plan changes to [Assignment: organization-defined key contingency personnel (identified by name and/or by role) and organizational elements]; and

(l) Protects the contingency plan from unauthorized disclosure and modification.

**CP-2 Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance:**

**Requirement:** For JAB authorizations the contingency lists include designated FedRAMP personnel.

## CP-4 Contingency Plan Testing (H)

The organization:

> (a) Tests the contingency plan for the information system [*FedRAMP Assignment: at least annually*] using [*FedRAMP Assignment: functional exercises*] to determine the effectiveness of the plan and the organizational readiness to execute the plan;

**CP-4(a) Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance:**

**Requirement:** The service provider develops test plans in accordance with NIST Special Publication 800-34 (as amended) and provides plans to FedRAMP prior to initiating testing. Test plans are approved and accepted by the JAB/AO prior to initiating testing.

(o) Reviews the contingency plan test results; and

(p) Initiates corrective actions, if needed.

## CP-7 Alternate Processing Site (M) (H)

> **CP-7a Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance:**
>
> **Requirement:** The service provider defines a time period consistent with the recovery time objectives and business impact analysis.

(q) Ensures that equipment and supplies required to transfer and resume operations are available at the alternate processing site or contracts are in place to support delivery to the site within the organization-defined time period for transfer/resumption; and

(r) Ensures that the alternate processing site provides information security safeguards equivalent to that of the primary site.

The first backup job session always produces a full backup of the VM image. Subsequent backup job sessions are incremental. Veeam Backup &amp; Replication copies only those data blocks that have changed since the last backup job session. Backup jobs are scheduled each day at a specific time. Veeam updates the backup image to reflect the current user-level data. VGC handles and retains user information, data, and log information for 14 days on disk. After the 14 days, the information is transferred via Nimble replication from the Main Nimble Storage server to the Archival Storage server. Select customers my request longer term offline retention (90 days) via virtual tapes, however this is optional and not part of the standard VGC offering. Veeam and Nimble, respectively backs up and replicates both Linux and Windows servers. Per VGC Customer Request, VGC backs up customer application information and database information. VGC System Administrator maintains three backup copies of user-level information: 1) Disk (online for 14 days), 2) Backup copy transfer from Main Shared Storage to Archival Storage (as depicted on *VGC Network Diagrams 20170802_updated*) and optionally, virtual tape (offline for 90 days) and, 3) Replicated virtual hosts from Primary to DR Site. The backup storage capability is approved and accepted by the JAB.<br/><br/>**IL4 Implementation:** Same as VGC implementation.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>Part b</td>
        <td rowspan="2">Implemented<br/><br/>**Shared (Service Provider and Customer Responsibility)**<br/><br/>**VGC:** VGC System Administrators conduct Daily Incremental Backups and Weekly Full Backups for system-level information contained within VGC. There are two types of backups: system state backups and data backups, which are conducted at the request of the VGC Customer. System state backups capture the state of the system at a specific time of day. Should a system fail, it would be easy to reconfigure because the last current state of the system is preserved. The data backups are added to the new server and therefore, production resumes. These are scheduled each day at a specific time. Veeam updates the backup image to reflect the current system-level information. VGC handles and retains system information, data, and log information for 14 days on disk. After the 14 days, the information is transferred via Nimble replication from the Main Nimble Storage server to the Archival Storage server. Select customers my request longer term offline retention (90 days) via virtual tapes, however this is optional and not part of the standard VGC offering. Veeam and Nimble, respectively backs up and replicates both Linux and Windows servers. Per VGC Customer Request, VGC backs up customer application information and database information. VGC System Administrator maintains three backup copies of system-level information: 1) Disk (online for 14 days), 2) Backup copy transfer from Main Nimble Shared Storage to Nimble Archival Storage (as depicted in *VGC Network Diagrams 20170802_updated*) and optionally, virtual tape (offline for 90 days) and, 3) Replicated virtual hosts from Primary to DR Site. After the 14 days, the information is transferred offline (incremental daily and full weekly tapes) and retained on backup tapes for 90 days at the Cyxtera media storage DC6 data center. In addition, the DR site located at the Cyxtera disaster recovery DN1 and Equinix SV1 data centers, which has copies of critical files to ensure the availability of the site in case the primary site goes down. Veeam backs up both</td>

The VGC System Administrator maintains three backup copies of information system documentation: 1) VGC Primary Internal FedRAMP OneDrive repository 2) VGC Box Repository and, 3) DR Site. The backup storage capability is approved and accepted by the JAB.<br/>**IL4 Implementation:** DoD-affiliated agency customer will describe how it conducts backups of information system documentation including security-related documentation when created or received, when updated, and as required by system baseline configuration changes in accordance with the contingency plan.<br/>**Customer Responsibility:** The VGC Customer is responsible for conducting backups of application and database documentation including security-related documentation.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>Part d</td>
        <td>**Implemented**<br/>**Shared (Service Provider and Customer Responsibility)**<br/>**VGC:** VGC System Administrator protects the confidentiality and integrity of backup information at storage locations by implementing FIPS 140-2 cryptographic modules to provide protection for data-at-rest and data-in-transit and protects availability by implementing physical controls to prevent unauthorized access to the backup media, virtual servers, network devices, and security appliances within the VGC accreditation boundary. To protect confidentiality and integrity, the FTGS System Administrator configures Veeam which natively enables AES 256 cryptographic modules to encrypt the data that is being backed up. In addition, VGC System Administrator configures “fips mode” within Nimble to provide SAN-level encryption using AES 256 cryptographic module. AES 256 also encrypts data stored on virtual tapes attached to Veeam backup server . To prevent unauthorized access to backup media, VGC Program Manager leverages the physical and environmental security measures provided by Cyxtera and Equinix. These security measures include multi-factor access requirements to enter the data center and authorization to request the secured cage and cabinets where the backup media is located to be opened by a cleared Cyxtera or Equinix data center engineer. The data center monitors the HVAC, Power, and other environmental conditions to ensure there is no service interruption.<br/>**IL4 Implementation:** Same as VGC implementation.<br/>**Customer Responsibility:** The VGC Customer will describe in its SSP how it protects the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of backup information at storage locations for the database and application.</td>

        <td>**Implemented**<br/><br/>**Service Provider Corporate**<br/><br/>**VGC:** VGC tests backup information at least annually to verify media reliability and information integrity. VGC System Administrator use Veeam SureBackup to test VM backups. SureBackup lets us test VM backups and make sure that data is recover from target VMs. Veeam Backup &amp; Replication performs “live” verification of the VM backup: it automatically boots the VM from the backup in the isolated environment, performs tests for the VM, powers the VM off and creates a report about the recovery verification results. Performing this test allows us to verify the latest restore point of the backup or any other restore point. VGC DR site in Highlands Ranch, CO has mirrored configurations of the primary site. The VGC System Administrator tests backup information by cutting over from the primary site to the DR Site and then reviewing the components and configurations within the VGC DR Site. ### IA-3 (1) Control Enhancement (IL4)
The information system authenticates *[Assignment: organization-defined specific devices and/or types of devices]* before establishing *[Selection (one or more): local; remote; network]* connection using bidirectional authentication that is cryptographically based.

Supplemental Guidance: A local connection is any connection with a device communicating without the use of a network. A network connection is any connection with a device that communicates through a network (e.g., local area or wide area network, Internet). A remote connection is any connection with a device communicating through an external network (e.g., the Internet). Bidirectional authentication provides stronger safeguards to validate the identity of other devices for connections that are of greater risk (e.g., remote connections). Related controls: SC-8, SC-12, SC-13.

    <tr>
        <td>VGC: For devices within the VGC, the Network Administrator, Security Engineer, and Security Analyst maintain a list of System Names, Devices/Device Names, and Numbers in OneDrive, so that when a new system is built, the system names, devices, and numbers are not replicated for at least two years. This list is maintained indefinitely. Windows accounts correspond to security identifiers (SID). A SID is used to uniquely identify a security principal or security group. Security principals can represent any entity that can be authenticated by the operating system, such as a user account, a computer account, or a thread or process that runs in the security context of a user or computer account.<br/>Each account, group, or process running in the security context of the account, has a unique SID that is issued by an authority (i.e. Windows domain controller). The system generates the SID that identifies a particular account or group at the time the account or group is created. When a SID has been used as the unique identifier for a user or group, it can never be used again to identify another user or group.<br/>Each time a user signs in, the system creates an access token for that user. The access token contains the user’s SID, user rights, and the SIDs for any groups the user belongs to. This token provides the security context for whatever actions the user performs on that computer. SIDs are a fundamental building block of the Windows security model. They work with specific components of the authorization and access control technologies in the security infrastructure of the Windows Server operating systems. This helps protect access to network resources and provides a more secure computing environment.<br/>SIDs are unique within their scope (domain or local), and they are never reused.<br/>The operating system generates a SID that identifies a particular account or group at the time the account or group is created. The SID for a local account or group is generated by the Local Security Authority (LSA) on the computer, and it is stored with other account information in a secure area of the registry. The SID for a domain account or group is generated by the domain security authority, and it is stored as an attribute of the User or Group object in Active Directory Domain Services.<br/>For every local account and group, the SID is unique for the computer where it was created. No two accounts or groups on the computer ever share the same SID. Likewise, for every domain account and group, the SID is unique within an enterprise. This means that the SID for an account or group that is created in one domain will never match the SID for an account or group created in any other domain in the enterprise.<br/>SIDs always remain unique. Security authorities never issue the same SID twice, and they never reuse SIDs for deleted accounts. For example, if a user with a user account in a Windows domain leaves her job, an administrator deletes her Active Directory account, including the SID that identifies the account. If she later returns to a different job at the same company, an administrator creates a new account, and the Windows Server operating system generates a new SID. The new SID does not match the old one; so none of the user’s access from her old account is transferred to the new account. Her two accounts represent two completely different security principals. Further analysis on SIDs are found at the following Microsoft URL: https://technet.microsoft.com/en-us/library/dn743661(v=ws.11).aspx.<br/>**IL4 Implementation:** Same as VGC implementation.<br/>**Customer Responsibility:** The VGC Customer is responsible for preventing reuse of user identifiers for the application and database.</td>
        <td></td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

## IA-5 Authenticator Management (L) (M)

The organization manages information system authenticators by:

(a) Verifying, as part of the initial authenticator distribution, the identity of the individual, group, role, or device receiving the authenticator;

(a) Establishing initial authenticator content for authenticators defined by the organization;

(b) Ensuring that authenticators have sufficient strength of mechanism for their intended use;

(c) Establishing and implementing administrative procedures for initial authenticator distribution, for lost/compromised or damaged authenticators, and for revoking authenticators;

(d) Changing default content of authenticators prior to information system installation;

(e) Establishing minimum and maximum lifetime restrictions and reuse conditions for authenticators;

(f) Changing/refreshing authenticators [*FedRAMP Assignment: to include sixty (60) days for passwords*].

(g) Protecting authenticator content from unauthorized disclosure and modification;

(h) Requiring individuals to take, and having devices implement, specific security safeguards to protect authenticators; and

(i) Changing authenticators for group/role accounts when membership to those accounts changes.

### IA-5 (1) Control Enhancement (L) (M)
The information system, for password-based authentication:
(a) Enforces minimum password complexity of *[FedRAMP Assignment: case sensitive, minimum of twelve (12) characters, and at least one (1) each of upper-case letters, lower-case letters, numbers, and special characters]*;
(a) Enforces at least the following number of changed characters when new passwords are created: *[FedRAMP Assignment: at least one (1)]*;
(b) Stores and transmits only cryptographically-protected passwords;
(c) Enforces password minimum and maximum lifetime restrictions of *[FedRAMP Assignment: one (1) day minimum, sixty (60) day maximum]*;

(d) Prohibits password reuse for [FedRAMP Assignment: twenty-four (24)] generations; and
(e) Allows the use of a temporary password for system logons with an immediate change to a permanent password.

### IA-5 (2) Control Enhancement (M) (H)
The information system, for PKI-based authentication:
(a) Validates certifications by constructing and verifying a certification path to an accepted trust anchor including checking certificate status information;
(b) Enforces authorized access to the corresponding private key;
(c) Maps the authenticated identity to the account of the individual or group; and

(d) Implements a local cache of revocation data to support path discovery and validation in case of inability to access revocation information via the network.

        <td>**Implemented**<br/>**Shared (Service Provider and Customer Responsibility)**<br/>**VGC:** VGC validates certificates by constructing a certification path with status information to an accepted trust anchor. The VGC Domain Administrator first creates the Enterprise Root CA via Active Directory Certificate Services Server Role on the domain controller. This process establishes the Enterprise Root CA as the trust anchor of the certification chain. Additionally, the Enterprise Root CA establishes the certificate policy and the certificate revocation list. A user or device validates certificate details such as: version, signature algorithm, serial number, validity dates, RSA key-length, etc. by viewing the certificate properties. In addition, a user or device can see the certification path from the certificate itself all the way to the root CA confirming that certificate originated from a trusted anchor.<br/>**Customer Responsibility:** The VGC Customer is responsible for describing in its SSP how its applications and databases validate certificates by constructing a certification path with status information from an accepted trust anchor. The VGC Customer will receive certificates for any services requiring the use of certificates within the VGC private network. For any public-facing services that require certificates, the VGC Customer would use a third-party certificate authority.</td>
    </tr>

An example of auto-enrollment would be the creation of a new user account in active directory. When the new user first logs into the domain a user certificate is automatically issued to that user. That user certificate is associated with that unique user. As part of the automatic issuance of the user certificate, a private key is assigned to that user account. The VGC system enforces authorized access to the user’s corresponding private key by the user successfully or unsuccessfully logging on. If the user’s logon attempt is unsuccessful, then there is a mismatch between the user account and the private key.<br/>**Customer Responsibility:** The VGC Customer is responsible for describing in its SSP how its applications and databases enforce authorized access to the private key. This process will be the same for the VGC Customer as it is described for the VGC, however it will apply to public-facing services that require certificates, and the VGC Customer would use a third-party certificate authority.</td>
    </tr>

Additionally, the Enterprise Root CA establishes the certificate policy and the certificate revocation list.<br/>The enterprise root CA is installed on the domain controller which provides central management of certificates. ### IR-6 (1) Control Enhancement (M) (H)
The organization employs automated mechanisms to assist in the reporting of security incidents.

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
        <th>IR-6 (1)</th>
        <th>Control Summary Information</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
        <td colspan="2">Responsible Role: VGC Security Engineers, VGC Customer</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td colspan="2">Implementation Status (check all that apply):<br/>[x] Implemented<br/>[ ] Partially implemented<br/>[ ] Planned<br/>[ ] Alternative implementation<br/>[ ] Not applicable</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td colspan="2">Control Origination (check all that apply):<br/>[ ] Service Provider Corporate<br/>[ ] Service Provider System Specific<br/>[ ] Service Provider Hybrid (Corporate and System Specific)<br/>[ ] Configured by Customer (Customer System Specific)<br/>[ ] Provided by Customer (Customer System Specific)<br/>[x] Shared (Service Provider and Customer Responsibility)<br/>[ ] Inherited from pre-existing FedRAMP Authorization for Click here to enter text. , Date of Authorization</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
        <th>IR-6 (1) What is the solution and how is it implemented?</th>
        <th></th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
        <td colspan="2">**Implemented**<br/><br/>**Shared (Service Provider and Customer Responsibility)**<br/><br/>**VGC:** VGC Security Engineers use Splunk to automatically assist in reporting security incidents. EM7 monitors servers and networking devices by performing health checks and alerting system administrators and security engineers to take corrective actions. BigFix alerts engineers/administrators when patches are out of date and need updating, or if there is a failing hardware component. In addition, BigFix provides solutions to help administrators/engineers remediate the problem. EM7 monitors servers and networking devices by performing preconfigured service checks. EM7 checks for things such as hard drive capacity, CPU and memory utilization; for each service check, VGC system administrators define a threshold. If any of those thresholds are met, an administrator and engineer receive an alert to implement corrective actions (i.e., adding more hard drive space if device nears capacity). To identify unauthorized use of the system, VGC System Administrators implement Centrify and, at the host-level, Trend Micro (an intrusion detection system). Centrify monitors and captures keystrokes. Splunk monitors logs to keep track of all logon attempts (successful/unsuccessful attempts. Trend Micro provides alerts to all attempts to log into a host system). System Administrators also access Event Viewer to investigate unsuccessful login attempts.<br/><br/>**Customer Responsibility:** The VGC Customer is responsible for employing automated mechanisms to assist in the reporting of security incidents.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

## IR-9 Information Spillage Response (M) (H)

(d) Eradicating the information from the contaminated information system or component;
(e) Identifying other information systems or system components that may have been subsequently contaminated; and
(f) Performing other [*Assignment: organization-defined actions*].

## MA-2 Controlled Maintenance (L) (M) (H)
The organization:
(a) Schedules, performs, documents, and reviews records of maintenance and repairs on information system components in accordance with manufacturer or vendor specifications and/or organizational requirements;
(b) Approves and monitors all maintenance activities, whether performed on site or remotely and whether the equipment is serviced on site or removed to another location;
(c) Requires that *[Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles]* explicitly approve the removal of the information system or system components from organizational facilities for off-site maintenance or repairs;

(d) Sanitizes equipment to remove all information from associated media prior to removal from organizational facilities for off-site maintenance or repairs;
(e) Checks all potentially impacted security controls to verify that the controls are still functioning properly following maintenance or repair actions; and
(f) Includes [Assignment: organization-defined maintenance-related information] in organizational maintenance records.

The Security Engineer compares each log entry with a corresponding trouble ticket that authorized the remote access. Remote access entries without corresponding trouble tickets are investigated for unauthorized access.<br/><br/>**Customer Responsibility:** The VGC Customer is responsible for authorizing, monitoring, and controlling non-local maintenance and diagnostic activities for the application and database.</td>

Because AD is linked to the RSA Server that manages the RSA hardware token, the Cisco AnyConnect VPN (TLS Version 1.2) uses the RSA Server to verify identification by querying AD. The users launch the Cisco AnyConnect VPN and enter a user ID into the VPN client interface. The VGC System Administrator, Network Administrator, the Domain Administrator, Virtualization Administrator, and Security Engineer have a unique Security Identifier (SID) that is mapped to the user's name in AD.</td>

The authentication credentials are checked against those in AD. In Linux, `/etc/passwd` stores user names. Passwords are hashed and encrypted, and are stored in `/etc/shadow`. ## MA-5 (1) Control Enhancement (L) (M)
The organization:
(a) Implements procedures for the use of maintenance personnel that lack appropriate security clearances or are not U.S. citizens, that include the following requirements:
* (1) Maintenance personnel who do not have needed access authorizations, clearances, or formal access approvals are escorted and supervised during the performance of maintenance and diagnostic activities on the information system by approved organizational personnel who are fully cleared, have appropriate access authorizations, and are technically qualified;
* (2) Prior to initiating maintenance or diagnostic activities by personnel who do not have needed access authorizations, clearances or formal access approvals, all volatile information storage components within the information system are sanitized and all nonvolatile storage media are removed or physically disconnected from the system and secured; and

(b) Develops and implements alternate security safeguards in the event an information system component cannot be sanitized, removed, or disconnected from the system.

engineers and they need to go through a basic background check, a government issued I.D would be verified, and escorted by the authorized VGC personnel.<br/>The VGC personnel ensures that the vendor personnel only perform maintenance activities on the specific affected infrastructure component.<br/>**Customer Responsibility:** The VGC Customer will describe in its SSP how it implements procedures for the use of maintenance personnel that lack appropriate security clearances or are not U.S. citizens that include the following requirements.</td>
        <td></td>
    </tr>

        <td>Part b</td>
        <td>**Implemented**<br/>**Shared (Service Provider and Customer Responsibility)**<br/>**VGC:** The VGC Security Analyst develops and implements alternate security safeguards in the event an information system component cannot be sanitized, removed, or disconnected from the system. At the infrastructure and OS level, access control lists and firewall rules can be applied to firewalls, ports can be disabled, and OS level services can be turned off as security safeguards.<br/>**Customer Responsibility:** The VGC Customer will describe in its SSP how it develops and implements alternate security safeguards in the event an information system component cannot be sanitized, removed, or disconnected from the system. These would typically include database views, constrained interfaces, restricted user interfaces, and application partitioning.</td>

        <td>Part a</td>
        <td rowspan="2">**Implemented**<br/><br/>**Service Provider Corporate**<br/><br/>**VGC:** To detect and respond to physical security incidents, Cyxtera Security personnel monitor the Cyxtera CyberCenter hosting facility 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Video surveillance is used to monitor both the indoor and outdoor areas of the facility. Video surveillance cameras are also stationed on every aisle of the data center floor, so that security personnel can adequately monitor all areas. All entrances and exit doors of the facility are protected by automated alarm systems. Surveillance activity is stored on digital video, and is stored on-site for a minimum of 30 days. Per its colocation agreement with Cyxtera, VGC owns and assumes responsibility for this control.<br/><br/>In the event of a security incident related to physical access to the VGC system, Cyxtera Security personnel contacts The VGC Program Manager who in turn informs the VGC Security Engineer of the security incident. The VGC Security Engineer begins investigating the incident by initiating FTGS’ Incident Response Plan. In addition to inspecting the cabinet and physical servers and network components of the VGC environment, The VGC Security Engineer will request physical access logs from Cyxtera as part of the preparation stage of performing incident response. Further analysis of information and evidence gathered will allow the VGC Security Engineer to identify the scope of the security incident, to contain the security incident, to eradicate the security incident, and ultimately to recover from the security incident. The VGC Security Engineer will take detailed notes while going through the incident response process. To close out the incident, The VGC Security Engineer will write an incident report describing the incident, incident findings, and any recommendations and submit this report to the VGC Program Manager. This security incident report will be the key artifact that is used in a lessons learned exercise for FTGS employees.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>

        <td>**Implemented**<br/><br/>**Service Provider Corporate**<br/><br/>**VGC:** Cyxtera also has a Central Monitoring Center, which is tasked with monitoring alerts and reviewing logs semiannually from the Cyber Center’s Badging Access System. The VGC Security Engineer also reviews access logs from Cyxtera, semiannually, as part of Continuous Monitoring.<br/><br/>**IL4 Implementation:** Same as VGC implementation.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>Part c</td>
        <td>**Implemented**<br/><br/>**Service Provider Corporate**<br/><br/>**VGC:** Cyxtera Cyber Center personnel contacts the VGC Program Manager by email to coordinate results of reviews and investigations with the VGC SIRT Team. The VGC Program Manager along with the VGC SIRT Team further analyze the results of reviews and investigations to ascertain whether deeper analysis is required or to archive the results in the OneDrive document repository.</td>
    </tr>

defined information security topics];

### RA-3 Risk Assessment (L) (M)
The organization:
(a) Conducts an assessment of risk, including the likelihood and magnitude of harm, from the unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction of the information system and the information it processes, stores, or transmits;
(ff) Documents risk assessment results in [*Selection: security plan; risk assessment*]

report; [*FedRAMP Assignment: security assessment report*];

(gg) Reviews risk assessment results [*FedRAMP Assignment: in accordance with OMB A-130 requirements or when a significant change occurs*];

(hh) Disseminates risk assessment results to [*Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles*]; and

(ii) Updates the risk assessment [*FedRAMP Assignment: in accordance with OMB A-130 requirements or when a significant change occurs*] or whenever there are significant changes to the information system or environment of operation (including the identification of new threats and vulnerabilities), or other conditions that may impact the security state of the system.

**RA-3 Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance:**

**Guidance:** Significant change is defined in NIST Special Publication 800-37 Revision 1, Appendix F

**RA-3 (d) Requirement:** Include the Authorizing Official; for JAB authorizations to include FedRAMP.

## RA-5 Vulnerability Scanning (L) (M) (H)

The organization:

*   (a) Scans for vulnerabilities in the information system and hosted applications [*FedRAMP Assignment: monthly operating system/infrastructure; monthly web applications and databases*] and when new vulnerabilities potentially affecting the system/applications are identified and reported;
    *   **RA-5 (a) Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance:**
    *   **Requirement:** An accredited independent assessor scans operating systems/infrastructure, web applications, and databases once annually.
*   (jj) Employs vulnerability scanning tools and techniques that promote interoperability among tools and automate parts of the vulnerability management process by using standards for:
    *   (1) Enumerating platforms, software flaws, and improper configurations;
    *   (2) Formatting and making transparent, checklists and test procedures; and
    *   (3) Measuring vulnerability impact;
*   (kk) Analyzes vulnerability scan reports and results from security control assessments
*   (ll) Remediates legitimate vulnerabilities; [*FedRAMP Assignment: high-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within thirty (30) days from date of discovery; moderate risk vulnerabilities mitigated within ninety (90) days from date of discovery*], in accordance with an organizational assessment of risk; and
*   (mm) Shares information obtained from the vulnerability scanning process and security control assessments with [*Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles*] to help eliminate similar vulnerabilities in other information systems (i.e., systemic weaknesses or deficiencies).
    *   **RA-5 (e) Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance:**
    *   **Requirement:** To include the Risk Executive; for JAB authorizations to include FedRAMP ISSOs.

    <tr>
        <td>Part a</td>
        <td rowspan="2">**Implemented**<br/><br/>**Shared (Service Provider and Customer Responsibility)**<br/><br/>**VGC:** FTGS manages the information system using a system development life cycle methodology that includes information security considerations.<br/><br/>● **Initiation:** During the initiation phase, the need for a system is expressed and the purpose of the system is documented. Activities include conducting an impact assessment in accordance with FIPS-199 (http://csrc.nist.gov/publications/fips/fips199/FIPS-PUB-199-final.pdf). As part of the initiation phase a needs analysis is conducted and documented in a ServiceNow change request. Also included in the change request are operational requirements and functions allocated to the requirements as a result of a functional analysis.<br/><br/>● **Development/Acquisition:** During this phase, the system is designed, purchased, programmed, developed, or otherwise constructed. This phase often consists of other defined cycles, such as the system development cycle or the acquisition cycle. Activities include determining security requirements, incorporating security requirements into specifications, and obtaining the system. A key element is to ensure the operational and functional requirements will be met.<br/><br/>● **Implementation:** During implementation, the system is tested and installed or fielded.<br/><br/>● Activities include installing/turning on controls, security testing, certification, and accreditation. At the end of this phase, FTGS verifies that the operational and functional requirements were met and underlying needs have been achieved. For major changes, the 3PAO will conduct a risk assessment, the results of which go into a Security Assessment Report (SAR). Once this has been verified, the change request in ServiceNow is updated prior to closure.<br/><br/>● **Operation/Maintenance:** During this phase, the system performs its work. Typically, the system is also being modified by the addition of hardware and software and by numerous other events. Activities include security operations and administration, operational assurance, and audits and monitoring.<br/><br/>● **Disposal:** The disposal phase of the IT system life-cycle involves the disposition of information, hardware, and software. Activities include moving, archiving, discarding or destroying information and sanitizing the media.<br/><br/>**IL4 Implementation:** Same as VGC implementation.<br/><br/>**Customer Responsibility:** The VGC Customer is responsible for managing the application and database using a system development life cycle methodology that Includes information security considerations.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>Part b</td>
        <td>**Implemented**</td>
    </tr>

</table>

For the standard VGC deployment, the accreditation boundary will be comprised of a shared management zone (SMZ) which will only be accessible to FTGS administrators and engineers and will have the centralized VGC management tools. There is an encrypted VPN tunnel between the SMZ and the Customer CPM management zone. The Customer CPM management zone houses the collectors and agents that communicate with the managers that are installed on the SMZ management zone. For example the Splunk Indexer (manager) receives logs from the Customer CPM via the splunkforwarder (agent) that is installed in the Customer CPM management zone. There is a one-way trust between the Customer CPMs and the SMZ management zone such that communication is allowed from Customer CPM management zone to SMZ management zone but not from Customer CPM to Customer CPM. Customer CPM access is controlled by a Remote Desktop Server (Jumphost) located in the Customer CPM management zone. From the Jumphost, the Customer has access to the production zone of the CPM.</td>

(7) Known vulnerabilities regarding configuration and use of administrative (i.e., privileged) functions;

(b) Obtains user documentation for the information system, system component, or information system service that describes:
(8) User-accessible security functions/mechanisms and how to effectively use those security functions/mechanisms;
(9) Methods for user interaction, which enables individuals to use the system, component, or service in a more secure manner; and
(10) User responsibilities in maintaining the security of the system, component, or service;

(nn) Documents attempts to obtain information system, system component, or information system service documentation when such documentation is either unavailable or nonexistent and [Assignment: organization-defined actions] in response;

(oo) Protects documentation as required, in accordance with the risk management strategy; and

(pp) Distributes documentation to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles)].

  <tbody>
    <tr>
        <td>**Implemented**<br/><br/>**Shared (Service Provider and Customer Responsibility)**<br/><br/>**VGC:** The VGC Security Engineers follow the security principles documented in NIST SP 800-27.<br/><br/>(i) Developing layered protections. The VGC Authorization Boundary is connected to the Internet using multiple 10GB cross-connections that are attached to two layer 3 switches that are connected to L3 and Zayo network services. The layer 3 switches are configured in an active-standby state for seamless failover. In the event Layer 3 Switch 1 goes down, Layer 3 Switch 2 can take over the routing of traffic. This provides at least two Internet connection points.<br/><br/>All Customer Cloud Platform Modules (CCPMs) and the FastTrack Management Zone(MZ) are connected to the VGC Front Switch Stack, which defines the accreditation boundary. Site-to-site VPN’s are configured between the MZ firewall and the CCPM firewalls. Firewalls are configured as a high availability (HA) pair for redundancy.<br/><br/>The MZ Switches provide dedicated ports for storage and network connectivity. MZ ESXi hosts, ports 1 and 2 are assigned for network-related traffic (ex. Vmotion, management, VLAN traffic). Ports 3 and 4 are assigned for MZ SAN storage related traffic.<br/><br/>Dedicated CCPM firewalls form endpoints to their respective management zones, the FastTrack Management Zoneand CCPM Management Zone, using Cisco AnyConnect TLS Version 1.2 VPN (FIPS 140-2) over a secure tunnel. An additional layer of security is provided through the use of network address translation (NAT). NAT allows CPM users to authenticate to the CPM endpoint.<br/><br/>(ii) establishing sound security policy, architecture, and controls as the foundation for design;<br/><br/>FTGS establishes sound security policies and processes that address all NIST control families. In addition, FTGS has a CP, an IRP, CMP, and other policies and procedures to ensure the highest level of protection for the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the data.<br/><br/>(iv) delineating physical and logical security boundaries;<br/><br/>FTGS delineates physical and logical security boundaries for the VGC. For physical boundaries,</td>
        <td></td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<table>
    <tr>
        <th>SA-8 What is the solution and how is it implemented?</th>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>FTGS employs the services of Cyxtera and Equinix Data Centers to provide physical security protection for the VGC infrastructure. Cyxtera and Equinix provides a locked lobby door, a man trap, doors that require badge access, closed circuit video recording, locked cabinets, and contractor access badges. FTGS also implements logical security boundaries for the VGC infrastructure via ACLs, Group Policy, Attachment 10, Role Matrix, RSA-token enforced VPN, and VLANs.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;(v) Ensuring system developers and integrators are trained on how to develop secure software; This is N/A to FTGS. FTGS provides OS and infrastructure services.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;(vi) Tailoring security controls to meet organizational and operational needs; FTGS will request the permission of the Information System Owner if tailoring is necessary because it could potentially change the categorization of the system.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;(vii) Reducing risk to acceptable levels, thus enabling informed risk management decisions. FTGS conducts monthly Nessus scans to identify vulnerabilities within the system. Critical vulnerabilities are remediated before 30 days; HIGH vulnerabilities are remediated within 30 days and MODERATE vulnerabilities are remediated within 90 days. In addition, scans are also conducted outside of the aforementioned scan cycle per customer request. FTGS Security Engineers run scans after patches are applied, after a major configuration change, or after a major incident such as the Heartbleed notification from U-S Cert.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;**Customer Responsibility:** The VGC Customer is responsible for applying application and database security engineering principles in the specification, design, development, implementation, and modification of the information system.</td>
    </tr>

        <th>which provide additional security and separation of traffic destined to any servers or nodes that are associated with that particular network. VGC Network Administrators configure VLANs to access mode; this permits traffic to go to specific places; therefore</th>

<table>
    <tr>
        <th>SC-5 What is the solution and how is it implemented?</th>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>Network Administrators implement ‘threat detection’ functions on the MZ and CCPM Firewalls. Threat detection is enabled on both MZ and CCPM firewalls to monitor the rate of dropped packets and security events due to the following reasons:&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Denial by access lists&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Bad packet format (such as invalid-ip-header or invalid-tcp-hdr-length)&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Connection limits exceeded (both system-wide resource limits, and limits set in the configuration)&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● DoS attack detected (such as an invalid SPI, Stateful Firewall check failure)&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Suspicious ICMP packets detected&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Packets failed application inspection&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Interface overload&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Scanning attack detected (This option monitors scanning attacks; for example, the first TCP packet is not a SYN packet, or the TCP connection failed the 3-way handshake. Full scanning threat detection takes this scanning attack rate information and acts on it by classifying hosts as attackers and automatically shunning them.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Incomplete session detection such as TCP SYN attack detected or no data UDP session attack detected&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;When the firewalls detect a threat, it immediately sends a system log message (733100). The firewalls track two types of rates: the average event rate over an interval, and the burst event rate over a shorter burst interval. The burst rate interval is 1/30th of the average rate interval or 10 seconds, whichever is higher. For each received event, the firewalls check the average and burst rate limits; if both rates are exceeded, then the firewalls send two separate system messages, with a maximum of one message for each rate type per burst period.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;Firewall logs are forwarded to Splunk which is configured to send email alerts to the VGC Security Engineer and VGC Network engineer to investigate further.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;EM7 also provides complete bandwidth monitoring of switches and firewalls via SNMP. Switches and routers are monitored via SNMP version 3 and deliver bandwidth utilization for both inbound and outbound traffic and alert when specified thresholds are reached. In the event of a DoS/DDoS attack, the firewall automatically blocks the attacking host’s IP address to prevent flooding or bandwidth saturation, and EM7 would continually send critical email alerts to the VGC Network Administrator and the VGC Security Engineer until the alert is acknowledged and addressed.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;Additionally, each CPM has its own intrusion detection system (IDS) configured to perform near real-time monitoring, alerting and logging of anomalous traffic. If anomalous traffic is detected, the IDS sends an email notification alert to the FTGS Network Administrator, FTGS Security Administrator, and FTGS Security Engineer to investigate further. The list of denial of service attacks is accepted and approved by JAB.</td>
    </tr>
</table>

<table>
    <tr>
        <th>SC-6 What is the solution and how is it implemented?</th>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>**VGC:** At the VMware hypervisor level, the VGC Virtualization Administrator configures Distributed Resource Scheduler (DRS) to:&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Improve service levels by guaranteeing appropriate resources to virtual machines.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Deploy new capacity to a cluster without service disruption.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Automatically migrate virtual machines during maintenance without service disruption.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Monitor and manage more infrastructure per system administrator.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;In addition to limiting system resources by priority at the VMware virtualization layer, the VGC system limits system resources by priority at the virtual machine layer for both Windows and Linux servers.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;For Windows servers The VGC System Administrator limits the use of resources by priority for Windows servers by implementing Windows System Resource Manager (WSRM). With WSRM you can manage server processor and memory usage with standard or custom resource policies. Managing your resources can help ensure that all the services provided by a single server are available on an equal basis or that your resources will always be available to high-priority applications, services, or users.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;WSRM only manages processor resources when the combined processor load is greater than 70 percent. This means that it does not actively limit the resources that can be used by each consumer when processor load is low. When there is contention for processor resources, resource allocation policies help ensure minimum resource availability based on the management profile that you define. You can use WSRM to:&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Manage system resources (processor and memory) with preconfigured policies, or create custom policies that allocate resources per process, per user, per Remote Desktop Services session, or per Internet Information Services (IIS) application pool.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Use calendar rules to apply different policies at different times without manual intervention or reconfiguration.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Automatically select resource policies that are based on server properties and events (such as cluster events or conditions) or changes to installed physical memory or number of processors.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Collect resource usage data locally or in a custom SQL database. Resource usage data from multiple servers can be consolidated on a single computer running WSRM.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Create a computer group to help organize Remote Desktop Session Host (RD Session Host) servers that you want to manage. Policies can easily be exported or modified for an entire computer group.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;Because Windows Server 2012 R2 is designed to give as many resources as possible to non-operating system tasks, a server running a single role usually does not require resource management. However, when multiple applications and services are installed on a single server, they are not aware of competing processes. An unmanaged application or service will typically use all available resources to complete a task. Thus, it is important to use a tool such as WSRM to manage system resources on</td>
    </tr>
</table>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
        <th>SC-6 What is the solution and how is it implemented?</th>
        <th colspan="14"></th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
        <td>multipurpose servers. Using Windows System Resource Manager provides two key benefits:<br/><br/>● More services can run on a single server because service availability can be improved through dynamically managed resources.<br/><br/>● High-priority users or system administrators can access the system even during times of maximum resource load.<br/><br/>For Linux servers</td>
        <td>Most processes are started at the same priority level and the Linux kernel schedules time for each task evenly on the processor. Have a CPU intensive process that can be run at a lower priority? Then you need to tell the scheduler about it. There are at least three ways in which you can control how much CPU time a process gets:<br/><br/>● Use the “nice” command to manually lower the task’s priority. The “nice” command tweaks the priority level of a process so that it runs less frequently. This is useful when you need to run a CPU intensive task as a background or batch job. The niceness level ranges from -20 (most favorable scheduling) to 19 (least favorable). Processes on Linux are started with a niceness of 0 by default. The nice command (without any additional parameters) will start a process with a niceness of 10. At that level the scheduler will see it as a lower priority task and give it less CPU resources.<br/><br/>● Use the “cpulimit” command to repeatedly pause the process so that it doesn’t exceed a certain limit. The “cpulimit” tool curbs the CPU usage of a process by pausing the process at different intervals to keep it under the defined ceiling. It does this by sending SIGSTOP and SIGCONT signals to the process. It does not change the “nice” value of the process</td>
        <td>instead it monitors and controls the real-world CPU usage. “cpulimit” is useful when you want to ensure that a process doesn’t use more than a certain portion of the CPU. The disadvantage over “nice” is that the process can’t use all of the available CPU time when the system is idle.<br/><br/>● Use Linux’s built-in “control groups”</td>
        <td>a mechanism which tells the scheduler to limit the amount of resources available to the process. Control groups (cgroups) are a Linux kernel feature that allows you to specify how the kernel should allocate specific resources to a group of processes. With cgroups you can specify how much CPU time</td>
        <td>system memory</td>
        <td>network bandwidth</td>
        <td>or combinations of these resources can be used by the processes residing in a certain group. The advantage of control groups “nice” or “cpulimit” is that the limits are applied to a set of processes</td>
        <td>rather than to just one. Also</td>
        <td>“nice” or “cpulimit” only limit the CPU usage of a process</td>
        <td>whereas cgroups can limit other process resources.<br/><br/>● For network devices</td>
        <td>when best-effort network or services is not sufficient VGC Network Administrator can implement Quality of Service (QoS) to provide different priority for different applications</td>
        <td>users</td>
        <td>or data flow or to provide guaranteed level of performance for the specific data flow. QoS can improve with traffic-shaping techniques such as packet prioritizations</td>
        <td>application classifications</td>
        <td>and queuing at the congestion point.<br/><br/>**IL4 Implementation:** Same as VGC implementation.<br/><br/>**Customer Responsibility:** The VGC Customer is responsible for limiting the use of resources by priority for the application and database.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

        <th>SC-8 (1) What is the solution and how is it implemented?</th>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>● Communication between RDP Server and Windows&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;o Windows 2012 R2 FIPS Compliant Option for RDP&lt;br/&gt;● Communication between RDP Server and Linux&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;o Secure Shell (SSH) Version 2 using AES-256&lt;br/&gt;● Communication between Trend Micro agents and Trend Micro Manager&lt;br/&gt;● Communications from server and network devices to Splunk&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;To support integrity of the transmission, VGC only uses AnyConnect VPN TLS Version 1.2 to establish VPN between remote administrator client and the firewall. AnyConnect VPN Client uses TLS Version 1.2 to create a secure, encrypted tunnel to transmit the data and to protect the endpoints. Windows 2012R2 and Linux Servers both use Kerberos Version 5 for authentication. FIPS 140-2 processing is enabled on the group policy for the AD Domain controllers. This mode uses AES-256, Cipher Text Block Chaining with SHA-2 for hashing.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;The following are reference to FIPS 140-2 Certificates:&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;● Windows 2012R2, Certificate #1747&lt;br/&gt;● Cisco ASA, Consolidated Certificate #0028&lt;br/&gt;● Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6.2 dm-crypt Cryptographic Module v2.0, Certificate #1933&lt;br/&gt;● AnyConnect VPN, Certificate #407&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;The VGC System Administrator, VGC Network Administrator, and VGC Security Engineer configure logging and alerting on VGC system and network components to support transmission integrity. Local Trend Micro agents are installed on all servers, and remote Trend Micro agents are installed on network devices in order to perform the following integrity checks: file integrity checking, policy monitoring, and rootkit detection. VGC System Administrators configure servers running the Trend Micro agent to send real-time alerts via email for any changes to non-kernel-level files and configuration settings. For kernel-level files and configuration settings VGC System Administrators configure Trend Micro’s active response capability to prevent changes that would adversely affect the integrity of the system. To do this, VGC System Administrators define different threshold values for changes to the VGC system components. Non-kernel-level changes are assigned lower threshold values, while kernel-level changes are assigned high threshold values. VGC System Administrators, VGC Network Administrators, and VGC Security Engineers review system, network, and security alerts respectively, giving highest priority and responding appropriately based on the type of alert and its threshold value.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;The Trend Micro agents that are installed on each server within the VGC system communicate with the Trend Micro manager, which is installed on the Splunk server. This configuration streamlines alerting to allow for fast response to alerts that are assigned a high threshold value, while centralizing log collection to facilitate security analysis while performing security investigations.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;VGC Network Administrators configure all inbound connections into the VGC authorization boundary through a secure VPN tunnel using TLS Version 1.2 with AES-256 encryption and IKE Version 2 using AES-256 encryption. In the event transmission confidentiality cannot be achieved through cryptographic mechanisms, FTGS will work with the specific Government customer to determine the appropriate PDS for their needs.</td>
    </tr>
</table>

[thead]SC-12 What is the solution and how is it implemented?
**Implemented**<br/>**Service Provider Corporate**<br/><br/>**VGC:** The VGC System Administrator establishes and manages cryptographic keys within the VGC system. The cryptographic modules that are implemented in VGC are RSA SecurID and cryptographic modules derived by using Linux SSH key generator (ssh-keygen).

<table>
    <tr>
        <th>SC-12 What is the solution and how is it implemented?</th>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>RSA SecurID establishes and manages cryptographic keys by implementing the RSA asymmetric cryptographic module, which produces private and public keys, along with a pseudo-random number generating engine (PRNG), which uses an internal clock to change and manage the token seed (the numeric passcode that appears on the hardware token and changes at a defined time interval). The seed is different for each token, and is managed by the RSA SecurID server (RSA Authentication Manager).&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;Linux: The VGC System Administrator establishes and manages cryptographic keys by using the SSH-key generator (ssh-keygen) tool. To do this, the VGC System Administrator invokes “ssh-keygen” command at the Linux command line to initiate creation of the SSH private/public key-pair. To manage the generated keys, the VGC System Administrator selects a location within the VGC system where the keys are to be stored. To provide additional security, The VGC System Administrator may define a passphrase to protect the private key. Once the keys are generated, the public key can be copied to other servers and devices.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;**IL4 Implementation:** DoD-Affiliated agency customer establishes and manages cryptographic keys for required cryptography employed within the information system in accordance with DoDI 8520.02 "Public Key Infrastructure and Public Key Enabling" and DoDI 8520.03 "Identity Authentication for Information Systems".</td>
    </tr>

    <tr>
        <td>**Service Provider Corporate**&lt;br/&gt;**VGC:** FTGS domain administrators configure Active Directory. Keys are produced, controlled, and distributed in the following manner:&lt;br/&gt;The client authenticates itself to the Authentication Server (AS), which forwards the username to a key distribution center (KDC). The KDC issues a ticket granting ticket (TGT), which is time stamped, encrypts it using the user's password, and returns the encrypted result to the user's workstation.&lt;br/&gt;When the client needs to communicate with another node, the client sends the TGT to the ticket granting service (TGS), which usually shares the same host as the KDC. After verifying the TGT is valid and the user is permitted to access the requested service, the TGS issues a ticket and session keys, which are returned to the client. The client then sends the ticket to the service server (SS) along with its service request. This cryptographic module has been validated as conforming to the Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code (HMAC), as specified in Federal Information Processing Standard Publication 198, Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code (HMAC) and is on the NIST Validation List found at http://csrc.nist.gov/groups/STM/cavp/documents/mac/hmacval.html.&lt;br/&gt;**IL4 Implementation:** DoD-Affiliated agency customer produces, controls, and distributes symmetric cryptographic keys using NIST Approved for Unclassified systems, NSA Approved for Classified systems key management technology and processes.</td>
    </tr>

        <th>SC-17 What is the solution and how is it implemented?</th>

    <tr>
        <td>**Shared (Service Provider and Customer Responsibility)**</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
        <td>**VGC:** For internal services, VGC issues public key certificates through a single root certificate authority (CA) deployment. For external services the customer is responsible for obtaining public key certificates from an approved certificate authority.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;Internal services: The VGC Domain Administrator creates a public key infrastructure (PKI) consisting of software and hardware elements within each CPM boundary. For each CPM, the VGC Domain Administrator installs Active Directory Certificate Services (ADCS) server role on the domain controller via the Server Manager console. Stepping through the ADCS wizard, the VGC Domain Administrator selects "Certification Authority", "Enterprise", and "Root CA" in order to designate the domain controller as an Enterprise Root CA. The VGC Domain Administrator also defines the certificate policy through the ADCS wizard. The typical contents of the Enterprise Root CA certificate policy are comprised of the following components:&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;[Version]&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;Signature="$Windows NT$"&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;[PolicyStatementExtension]&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;Policies=InternalPolicy&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;[InternalPolicy]&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;OID= 1.2.3.4.1455.67.89.5&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;Notice="Legal Policy Statement"&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;URL=http://pki.fabrikam.com/cps.txt&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;[Certsrv_Server]&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;RenewalKeyLength=2048&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;RenewalValidityPeriod=Years&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;RenewalValidityPeriodUnits=20&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;AlternateSignatureAlgorithm=1&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;CRLDeltaPeriod=Days&lt;br/&gt;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;&amp;nbsp;CRLDeltaPeriodUnits=0&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;Once the Enterprise Root CA is configured, the VGC Domain Administrator creates group policies for auto-enrollment so that any components or services that require certificates are automatically issued a certificate. An example of auto-enrollment would be a computer that gets added to the domain and automatically receives a computer certificate that gets generated because of the computer group policy.&lt;br/&gt;&lt;br/&gt;In addition, the VGC Domain Administrator can add the Certification Authority Web Enrollment role within the domain controller. The CA Web Enrollment role service pages allow connection to the CA by using a web browser and performing common tasks, such as:&lt;br/&gt;1. Requesting certificates from the CA.&lt;br/&gt;2. Requesting the CA's certificate.&lt;br/&gt;3. Submitting a certificate request by using a PKCS #10 file.&lt;br/&gt;4. Retrieving the CA's certificate revocation list (CRL).&lt;br/&gt;The certificate policy is approved and accepted by the JAB.</td>

## SC-23 (3) Enhancement (IL4)
The information system generates a unique session identifier for each session with [Assignment: organization-defined randomness requirements] and recognizes only session identifiers that are system-generated.

**Supplemental Guidance:** This control enhancement curtails the ability of adversaries from reusing previously valid session IDs. Employing the concept of randomness in the generation of unique session identifiers helps to protect against brute-force attacks to determine future session identifiers. Related control: SC-13.

SC-23 (3) What is the solution and how is it implemented? [thead]
[colspan=1] **IL4 Implementation:** DoD-Affiliated agency customer systems are configured to generate a unique session identifier for each session with ASLR (address space layout randomization) randomness and Data Execution Prevention (DEP) and recognizes only session identifiers that are system-generated. Using ASLR and DEP curtails the ability of adversaries from reusing previously valid session IDs. Employing the concept of randomness in the generation of unique session identifiers helps to protect against brute-force attacks to determine future session identifiers. Both ASLR and DEP are kernel-level mechanisms that are not customer configurable.

        <th>SI-3 What is the solution and how is it implemented?</th>

  <tbody>
    <tr>
        <td>Part a</td>
        <td rowspan="2">**Implemented**<br/><br/>**Shared (Service Provider and Customer Responsibility)**<br/><br/>**VGC:** VGC employs malicious code protection mechanisms at information system entry and exit points and servers, on the network to detect and eradicate malicious code:<br/><br/>*   Transported by electronic mail, electronic mail attachments, web accesses, removable media, or other common means; or<br/>*   Inserted through the exploitation of information system vulnerabilities.<br/><br/>VGC system administrators configure Trend Micro antivirus on all servers to protect system entry and exit points at the server host level. The VGC System Administrator configures Trend Micro Deep Security web management console to centrally manage antivirus installations, apply virus definition updates and host intrusion prevention rule updates. The VGC System Administrator points Trend Micro Deep Security web management console to pull Security Rule updates (for Host Intrusion Prevention System) and Security Pattern updates (for antivirus definitions) from the Trend Micro Update Server. Trend Micro Deep Security requires VGC SMZ firewall and Customer CPM firewall ports TCP4118, TCP4120, TCP4122 to be open. VGC Network Administrator also updates the firmware on firewalls and applies security patches to the iOS to protect against known vulnerabilities. VGC Security Engineer conducts monthly Nessus vulnerability scans on firewalls and routers to identify any potential vulnerabilities on firewalls that would allow malicious code to enter the VGC environment. Based on the Nessus report, VGC Network Administrator makes the appropriate configuration changes to the firewall to provide maximum protection against malicious code at the entry and exit of the VGC system.<br/><br/>Additionally, because VGC system enforces RBAC, privileged access is restricted to only VGC administrators and VGC CPM Customer Administrators.<br/><br/>The VGC accreditation boundary does not have electronic mail configured.<br/><br/>**VGC Customer:** The VGC Customer is responsible for automatically configuring the scan for removable media to check for malicious code, and not allow access to perform any executable functions on it until the malicious code on the removable media has been quarantined or removed.</td>
    </tr>

        <td>**Implemented**<br/><br/>**Service Provider Corporate**<br/><br/>**VGC:** The VGC System Administrator configures agents, on all Windows and Linux servers in the VGC Accreditation boundary, to check the Trend Micro Deep Security Manager for new virus definitions and intrusion prevention rules on a daily basis. The FTGS System Administrator defines policies for downloading Rule updates and Pattern updates from the Trend Micro Download Center to the Trend Micro Deep Security Manager. These updates get pushed to all nodes via relays. VGC Network Administrator and VGC Security Engineer configures network devices and security appliances, respectively, to pull firmware updates and security patches from the vendor website, as updates and security patches become available or on a monthly basis.</td>

# SI-4 Information System Monitoring (L) (M) (H)

The organization:

(a) Monitors the information system to detect:
> (6) Attacks and indicators of potential attacks in accordance with [Assignment: organization-defined monitoring objectives]; and
> (7) Unauthorized local, network, and remote connections;

(d) Identifies unauthorized use of the information system through [Assignment: organization-defined techniques and methods];

(e) Deploys monitoring devices (i) strategically within the information system to collect organization-determined essential information; and (ii) at ad hoc locations within the system to track specific types of transactions of interest to the organization;

(f) Protects information obtained from intrusion-monitoring tools from unauthorized access, modification, and deletion;

(g) Heightens the level of information system monitoring activity whenever there is an indication of increased risk to organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, or the Nation based on law enforcement information, intelligence information, or other credible sources of information;

(h) Obtains legal opinion with regard to information system monitoring activities in accordance with applicable federal laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, or regulations; and

(ww) Provides [Assignment: organization-defined information system monitoring information] to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles] [Selection (one or more): as needed; [Assignment: organization-defined frequency]].

**SI-4 Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance:**

**Guidance:** See US-CERT Incident Response Reporting Guidelines.

        <td colspan="2">**Implemented**<br/>**Shared (Service Provider and Customer Responsibility)**<br/>**VGC:** VGC employs automated tools to support near real-time analysis of events. VGC System Administrators implement Centrify to capture keystrokes as users’ access servers within the VGC system. VGC System Administrators also configure Windows and Linux system logs to support near real-time analysis of events. Additionally, system administrators configure Trend Micro HIDS to automatically log anomalous events and alert system administrators and security engineers so that corrective action is taken. VGC uses EM7 to monitor servers and networking devices by performing health checks and alerting system administrators and security engineers to take corrective actions. EM7 monitors servers and networking devices by performing preconfigured service checks. EM7 checks for things such as hard drive capacity, CPU, and memory utilization; for each service check, VGC System Administrators and Security Engineers define a threshold. If any of those thresholds are met, an engineer receives an alert to take corrective action.<br/><br/>VGC Security Engineers configure FirePOWER NIDS/NIPS which supports near real-time analysis of intrusion detection events at the perimeter of the VGC system. Additionally, VGC Security Engineers configure Splunk to aggregate and analyze logs from the VGC system in order to capture the security posture of components within the accreditation boundary and take necessary action to strengthen it.<br/><br/>**Customer Responsibility:** The VGC Customer is responsible for employing automated tools to support near real-time analysis of events for the application and database.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

Furthermore, for systems that are in a shared environment, VGC implements VLANs that are configured to segregate traffic. VLAN-to-VLAN (inter-VLAN) traffic is monitored by the firewall, switch, and FirePOWER NIDS. Intra-VLAN (within a VLAN) traffic is monitored by FirePOWER NIDS. ## SI-10 (3) Control Enhancement (IL4)
The information system behaves in a predictable and documented manner that reflects organizational and system objectives when invalid inputs are received.

Supplemental Guidance: A common vulnerability in organizational information systems is unpredictable behavior when invalid inputs are received. This control enhancement ensures that there is predictable behavior in the face of invalid inputs by specifying information system responses that facilitate transitioning the system to known states without adverse, unintended side effects.

        <td>the DoD-Affiliated agency customer systems have ASLR to help prevent shellcode from being successful. It does this by randomly offsetting the location of modules and certain in-memory structures. In addition</td>
        <td>DEP – data execution prevention prevents certain (protected) memory sectors from being executed. For the application layer</td>
        <td>the agency customer would work with its application developer to ensure fail-safes - to protect its memory from unauthorized code execution - are in place.<br/><br/>**Customer Responsibility:** The VGC Customer will describe in its SSP how the information system implements safeguards to protect its memory from unauthorized code execution for the database and application.</td>
    </tr>

# ATTACHMENT 5 - RULES OF BEHAVIOR

All Authorization Packages must include a Rules of Behavior (RoB) attachment, which will be reviewed for quality.

The RoB describes controls associated with user responsibilities and certain expectations of behavior for following security policies, standards and procedures. Security control PL-4 requires a CSP to implement rules of behavior.

The Rules of Behavior Template can be found on the following FedRAMP website page: Templates.

The Template provides two example sets of rules of behavior: one for Internal Users and one for External Users. The CSP should modify each of these two sets to define the rules of behavior necessary to secure their system.
